clue.text: Top publican of Essex ?

parts.note: the chief of the bar, its king, read as one word gives the name of a town in Essex

explanation.surface: A question about who runs the finest pub in the county of Essex.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as BAR KING, the king of the bar, a top publican; joined up it is a town in Essex, the county east of London.
explanation.definitionFit: The town lies in Essex, east London, and the phrase splits into a bar's monarch, a leading landlord.

clue.text: A mere East Anglian

parts.note: mere is not 'only' but a lake: a person from the Norfolk lake district

explanation.surface: Dismissing someone as just a person from eastern England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mere' seems to belittle, but it is a lake; the Norfolk Broads are shallow lakes in East Anglia, eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the Norfolk Broads, a lake region of eastern England, is so called.

clue.text: Can't be the corner house, can it ?

definitions.text: Can't be the corner house, can it ?

parts.words: Can't be the corner house, can it
parts.note: a building that is circular has no corners at all

explanation.surface: Doubting that a building is the house on the street corner.
explanation.walkthrough: A round building with a dome has no corners, so it can never be a corner house.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular domed building has no angles, so it could never sit as a cornered house.

clue.text: It has a black record

parts.note: not a criminal history: a dark liquid used for writing and drawing

explanation.surface: Something with a shady past or criminal history.
explanation.walkthrough: 'black record' sounds like a criminal past; the answer is a black drawing liquid that records.
explanation.definitionFit: A dense black pigment used for drawing and writing leaves a dark mark on paper.

clue.text: To Georgia by donkey

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation of the US state
taken as written

explanation.surface: Travelling to the state of Georgia on a donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'donkey' is not transport but a fool; the answer is an old dialect word for a simpleton.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are slang for a simpleton or fool.

clue.text: Go back in, I call wildly, as is reasonable

indicators.note: in says the turned-round word goes inside the rearranged letters
wildly tells us the letters of I call are thrown into a new order
back tells us the word go is to be read in the opposite direction

explanation.surface: Someone urges a return indoors while shouting excitedly, and claims this is sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns GO into OG; 'wildly' rearranges I CALL into LICAL; 'in' puts OG inside after the L. 'as is' only links.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sensible and following sound argument is both reasonable and in keeping with logic.

clue.text: It does not turn out print frocks

definitions.text: It does not turn out print frocks

parts.words: It does not turn out print frocks
parts.note: this press holds cloth rather than printing on it: a cupboard for sheets

explanation.surface: A printing press that does not produce patterned dresses.
explanation.walkthrough: A press usually prints, but this one is a cupboard where household cloth is stored.
explanation.definitionFit: A cupboard for storing sheets and tablecloths is called a press of this kind.

clue.text: Hail with a Scots cry

explanation.surface: Welcoming someone with a Scottish shout.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scots the word means weep, so a 'cry' is tears, not a shout.
explanation.definitionFit: To hail someone is to welcome them; in Scots dialect the same word means to weep.

clue.text: An equal of those who are more equal than others?

definitions.text: An equal of those who are more equal than others?

parts.words: An equal of those who are more equal than others
parts.note: Orwell's more equal ones suggest lords of the realm; a companion of equal rank

explanation.surface: Someone who matches the privileged elite of Animal Farm.
explanation.walkthrough: Orwell's Animal Farm had some animals 'more equal than others'; peers are lords, and the answer contains a peer and means an equal.
explanation.definitionFit: A companion of equal standing, a fellow, is an old word containing peer.

clue.text: Surveyor's landscape

parts.note: Surveyor was the name of American probes sent to the Moon

explanation.surface: The terrain mapped by a land surveyor.
explanation.walkthrough: The Surveyor probes landed on the Moon in the 1960s, so their scenery was the moonscape.
explanation.definitionFit: The terrain the US Surveyor probes saw belonged to the Moon.

clue.text: Beefy fellow, comes from Surrey

parts.note: an ox is a beast that supplies beef
Ted is a common short man's name, a fellow

explanation.surface: A burly man turns out to hail from the county of Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: OXTED is a town in Surrey, the county south of London; 'Beefy' reads as burly but is the animal that gives beef.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer names a town in that county, so it is a place in Surrey.

clue.text: The ensign of the Campbells

explanation.surface: A flag-bearer for the Scottish clan Campbell.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman was a British prime minister, so the word follows 'Campbell' in his name.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensign carries the standard, a flag-bearer; and the prime minister's surname was Campbell-hyphen-this.

clue.text: Dancer at the court of Scotland

explanation.surface: A performer dancing at the Scottish royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: Isadora Duncan was a famous American dancer; Duncan was the Scottish king murdered by Macbeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Isadora of that surname was a celebrated modern dancer, and a Scottish king of that name held court.

clue.text: From Newark it comes — or Cardigan?

indicators.note: comes, after from, says new material is made out of the letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Asking whether some garment was made in the town of Newark or in Cardigan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardigan' looks like the Welsh town set beside Newark, but it is the woollen jacket, an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A cardigan is a buttoned woollen jacket, one example of garments made on needles.

clue.text: P.O.W. tot in Germany grown up in a cave

parts.note: with in Germany, a German camp for prisoners of war was a stalag
a mite is a tiny child, a tot

explanation.surface: A small child held in a German prisoner-of-war camp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in Germany' tells you the prisoner-of-war camp wanted is the German one.
explanation.definitionFit: The limestone spike that rises from a cave floor builds up over centuries.

clue.text: Warm resort for a shivering cold girl

definitions.text: Warm resort for a shivering cold girl

parts.words: Warm resort for a shivering cold girl
parts.note: a sunny Florida holiday town where a chilled young woman could warm up

explanation.surface: A frozen young woman needs a sunny holiday destination.
explanation.walkthrough: The cold girl is also Mimi of La Bohème, whose tiny hand is frozen: her name with A inside spells the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Florida city is a famous hot holiday destination, ideal for anyone feeling chilled.

clue.text: It's pitch dark as the interrupter of a pitched battle

definitions.text: It's pitch dark as the interrupter of a pitched battle

parts.words: It's pitch dark as the interrupter of a pitched battle
parts.note: a cask full of black pitch, such as might be set alight or rolled into a fight

explanation.surface: Something black as night that breaks up a set-piece battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pitch dark' means utterly black, but here pitch is the tar the cask holds, which is dark.
explanation.definitionFit: A cask used to hold tar or pitch, a black sticky substance, is so named.

clue.text: He's backing Britain!

parts.note: a supporter of the English and their country

explanation.surface: A slogan cheering on support for Britain.
explanation.walkthrough: Spelt here without its usual final E: a lover of all things English.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who admires and supports England and the English is so called.

clue.text: Parliament should — is it dragging its foot, then?

parts.note: the foot is at the end of a leg
taken as written
something dragging behind is late

explanation.surface: Grumbling that Parliament is slow, dragging its feet over making laws.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as LEG IS LATE: a limb that drags behind. 'it' and 'then' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: Parliament's job is to make laws, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: Don't they ever have headaches, even dull ones ?

definitions.text: Don't they ever have headaches, even dull ones ?

parts.words: Don't they ever have headaches, even dull ones
parts.note: heads without feeling feel no ache, and dull-witted people are so called

explanation.surface: Wondering whether some people never suffer from even a mild headache.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as NUMB SKULLS, heads too deadened to ache; as one word it means stupid people, the 'dull ones'.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull-witted people, blockheads, are so called, and a deadened head would feel no pain.

clue.text: Main force

parts.note: main is the old word for the open sea, so this is a sea-going force

explanation.surface: The principal body of an army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like principal, but it is the open sea; soldiers who serve at sea are the force.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers serving with the navy at sea make up a sea-borne fighting corps.

clue.text: No gig is, if it's broken down of course

indicators.note: broken down says the letters of no gig are smashed and rebuilt in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A carriage that has broken down is not moving anywhere, of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of course' is the definition, not a shrug: the condition of a racecourse's ground is described by this word.
explanation.definitionFit: The state of the ground on a racecourse, firm or soft, is called the going.

clue.text: I paced John from Scotland to Persia

definitions.note: a noun for the country where the answer is the adjective belonging to it

parts.note: ran means moved fast, paced
Ian is the Scottish form of John

explanation.surface: A man walks Ian all the way from Scotland to Persia.
explanation.definitionFit: Persia is the old name of Iran, so its people and things bear this adjective.

clue.text: Way from Victoria to Tilbury ?

parts.note: the London station and Thames port suggest a trip, but both are also kinds of horse-drawn vehicle

explanation.surface: Asking the route from Victoria station in London to Tilbury docks.
explanation.walkthrough: A victoria and a tilbury are both horse-drawn vehicles; the answer covers them all and also means conveyance, the way goods travel.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse-drawn vehicle such as a victoria or tilbury is one, and the word also means transport of goods.

clue.text: Poor Poe had extremely little credit for horse-sense

definitions.note: a noun for the knowledge that the person named by the answer, a horse-dealer, needs

indicators.note: the credit letters had, held, the shuffled Poe inside them

parts.note: credit cut to its first two letters, extremely little of it, gives the abbreviation CR

indicators.note: poor says the letters of Poe are in a bad, broken state

explanation.surface: The poet Edgar Allan Poe was given scant praise for common sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' shuffles POE to OPE, held by CR. 'horse-sense' is not common sense but the know-how of a horse-dealer.
explanation.definitionFit: A dealer in horses, who must judge them shrewdly, is an old term for one with horse-sense.

clue.text: The key of the tower ?

explanation.surface: Asking which key unlocks the tower.
explanation.walkthrough: A piano key is made of it, and an ivory tower is a retreat from the real world.
explanation.definitionFit: Piano keys were once made of elephant tusk, and an aloof academic retreat is called a tower of it.

clue.text: " We twa hae run about the braes, And pu'd the fine " (Burns)

definitions.text: " We twa hae run about the braes, And pu'd the fine " (Burns)

parts.words: We twa hae run about the braes, And pu'd the fine
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Burns's Auld Lang Syne: the missing word is the wild daisies the two friends picked

explanation.surface: A verse from Robert Burns's Auld Lang Syne with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: The line runs 'And pu'd the gowans fine': two friends picked daisies on the hillsides. 'Braes' are Scots hillsides.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots the daisy, the flower Burns's friends picked on the hillsides, is called by this name.

clue.text: He's the sort of chap who makes roots

definitions.text: He's the sort of chap who makes roots

parts.words: He's the sort of chap who makes roots
parts.note: a man's short name that is also a plant with roots

explanation.surface: Describing a man who is a natural at putting down roots.
explanation.walkthrough: Herb is a man's name, short for Herbert, and a herb is a plant that puts down roots.
explanation.definitionFit: A short form of Herbert is a man's name, and the plant of that name sends down roots.

clue.text: Principally transvestite show

parts.note: the British Christmas stage show where the principal boy is a woman and the dame a man

explanation.surface: A performance mostly about cross-dressing.
explanation.walkthrough: In a British Christmas panto the principal boy is played by a woman and the comic dame by a man, so its principals cross-dress.
explanation.definitionFit: The British family Christmas theatre show casts its principal boy and dame across the sexes.

clue.text: Exclaim if a port is seen

parts.note: ha is an exclamation of surprise or triumph
taken as written, the two words joined

explanation.surface: Someone cries out at the sight of a harbour.
explanation.definitionFit: The Israeli city is a seaport on the Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: Lets Rye give itself a new look

definitions.text: Lets Rye give itself a new look

indicators.note: the town giving itself a new look signals that its letters, with lets, are rearranged

explanation.surface: The Sussex town of Rye is permitted a makeover.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: the letters of LETS RYE take a new order, and the result means give a new look.
explanation.definitionFit: To redesign or freshen up something's appearance is to give it a different style.

clue.text: Stars of the high-wire act ?

explanation.surface: The headline performers of a tightrope circus act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stars' are not performers but a constellation: Libra, the Scales, is also called the Balance.
explanation.definitionFit: The constellation Libra is known as the Scales, and a tightrope walker depends on steadiness.
